md: Everything here is one seed of a 219K-parameter model on a synthetic task. Treat the numbers as a demonstration of the mechanism (more iterations resolve deeper chains, exits track depth, starts are forgotten), not as evidence about which adapter is better at scale.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA = frozen W0 + (alpha/r) B A, with B initialized to zero. You train r times (d + k) numbers per adapted matrix, and the model starts exactly at the pretrained one.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: Low scores on forget benchmarks show suppressed outputs, not erased knowledge. Small fine-tunes, probes and even 4-bit quantization can bring "forgotten" knowledge back, because approximate unlearning moves the weights only slightly.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Notarization, revocation and the Shlayer lesson
md: Notarization means "Apple's automated scan found nothing known-bad when this was uploaded". It is not a review of intent, and it can be fooled by code that only turns malicious later or hides its payload. Its real strength is speed of revocation once something is reported.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Case: Atomic Stealer and the paste-into-Terminal era
md: Resetting the user's password is not enough after a stealer. Session cookies stolen from the browser let the attacker into SaaS apps without the password or MFA until those sessions are revoked server-side.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The PE format: headers, sections and what imports reveal
md: Our benign hello.exe imports VirtualProtect and VirtualQuery even though main never calls them: the MinGW-w64 C runtime's startup code uses them. One 'suspicious' import proves nothing. Read imports as a combination, and check what the compiler's runtime adds.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Writing and testing YARA rules
md: A YARA rule is a hypothesis about what makes a family unique. The test set is the evidence. Keep the test files and expected results next to the rule, and rerun them on every change, just like unit tests.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search
md: The first stage must have high recall (it must not drop the right documents) and the last stage high precision (what it puts on top must be right). Matryoshka prefixes give a cheap high-recall first stage from the same vector the precise stage uses.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer and hiding communication behind compute
md: Overlap works because each collective has slack: gradients of late layers are ready early, and weights of the next layer are known before they are needed. What remains exposed is the last gradient bucket, the first parameter gather, and any collective on the critical path that cannot be chunked.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Acquiring RAM: WinPmem, DumpIt, LiME, AVML and virtual machines
md: Every acquisition changes the system it copies: the tool's process, its driver or module, and the memory they allocate all land in the image. LiME's README even warns that its optional digest and compression features disturb more of the target's memory. Record the tool, version, command and time so the footprint can be told apart from the attacker's.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Timelines from memory: what carries a time, and merging it
md: Memory gives you the start times of what is running now and a few remnants of what ran before. Disk gives you the long history. The overlap, a process in memory whose start matches a Prefetch run and a 4688 event, is where a timeline becomes solid.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging
md: Setting `dirty_decay_ms` to 0 is not a free fix. The manual says it purges dirty pages immediately when they are created, so every page that empties pays for a purge, and every later reuse pays a page fault. It lowers RSS that is merely waiting; it does nothing for pages pinned by live objects.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: A garbage collector does not make ABA impossible in every case. Michael points out that if a program moves the same live node back and forth between two lists, ABA can still occur even with perfect GC. What a GC (and the schemes in this course) guarantees is narrower: a node's address is not reused while someone can still reach it.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Grace periods (EBR, RCU) make reads cheap but let one stalled reader block all reclamation. Hazard pointers bound garbage at N x R but charge every visited node. Pick by read pattern and by how much you trust threads to keep moving.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Use-after-free and double free: dangling pointers
md: Chromium reports that about 70 percent of its high-severity security bugs are memory safety problems, and that half of those are use-after-free. Lifetimes are the hardest promise to keep by hand in a large C++ program.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Sample P identities x K images so every batch contains positives and look-alike negatives, then mine within the batch. Mining becomes a max and a min over a distance matrix you already have.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Misconception: "disabling ASLR and pinning the CPU makes my benchmark correct". They reduce run-to-run noise, which narrows intervals. A narrow interval around a biased setup is a confidently wrong answer.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Connecting an environment: rollout, generate and agent functions
md: Agent functions run in a child process of their own by default (`--custom-agent-function-mode subproc`), so one stuck episode cannot stall the others. The price: arguments and return values must be picklable, and module-level state lasts one call, so a module-level semaphore limits nothing. Use `rollout_semaphore` from `miles.rollout.agentic.rollout_limits`, or `inline` mode for debugging.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned policies leave a gap: LRU versus Belady's MIN
md: MIN is not a policy you can deploy, and it is not what learned caches try to predict exactly. It is a **yardstick**. Its value is telling you how big the gap is. On six production CDN traces with a 1 TB cache, the LRB authors measured a 25 to 40% gap in byte miss ratio (the fraction of requested bytes the cache could not serve) between MIN and the best online policies they tested.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Inside an APK and an IPA: what anyone can download and read
md: Legal note from the MASTG: in the US the DMCA (Digital Millennium Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. 1201) makes circumventing some DRM illegal, with exemptions for certain security research. On a client engagement, ask the developer for unencrypted builds; it is faster and removes the question.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The app is not the boundary: backend APIs seen through the app
md: A setting enforced only in the app's user interface is a display preference, not a privacy control. Test every privacy and permission setting by reading the raw API response.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Build an MLA layer and prove the two forms agree
md: Absorption is exact algebra, so a correct absorbed decoder matches the plain form to floating-point noise. Any larger gap is a bug, and the usual suspects are the norm, the RoPE split and the scale.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Thousands of adapters: S-LoRA's unified paging and loading
md: Unified Paging is not magic capacity. Adapter pages and KV pages come from the same pool, so many large adapters active at once shrink the space for KV cache and therefore the batch size. That is why clustering and rank choices still matter.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
md: Each stage has a different job. The first stage must not lose relevant documents (recall); precision barely matters there, because later stages discard junk. The last stage must put the best documents on top (precision at the top) and only has to be good on a short list.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: MTP reweights training toward decisions that matter for the continuation. It helps most on generative tasks such as code, at larger model sizes, with n tuned to the data; it is not a free win on every benchmark.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon = SGD with momentum + a post-processing step that equalizes the singular values of each 2D update, done with 5 bf16 Newton-Schulz iterations. Memory: one buffer. Extra compute: under 1% of a typical LLM training step.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
md: muP is not a formula that predicts the best SP learning rate for a bigger model. It changes how every layer's init and update scale with width, so a wide muP model trains differently from (and in the paper's experiments, better than) a wide SP model.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Verifying a muP implementation, and where muP stops
md: Before trusting muTransfer, run a coord check over a wide range of widths with a large learning rate. Flat curves after a few steps (apart from the output and attention logits at init) mean the parametrization is right.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
md: FUTEX_WAIT says "sleep only if the word still holds the value I based my decision on". That expected-value check, done atomically by the kernel, is what makes lost wake-ups impossible.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
md: Read Committed is not a weaker form of a single consistent view. Each statement sees one snapshot, but an updating statement can also see newer versions of the rows it is about to change, so a single UPDATE or DELETE can mix two moments in time. The docs call it unsuitable for commands with complex search conditions.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: BIO, IOB1 and BIOES: tag sets that make spans decodable
md: The repair rule is not cosmetic: it changes your score. [seqeval](https://github.com/chakki-works/seqeval) documents that for gold `B-NP I-NP O` and prediction `I-NP I-NP O`, its default mode (which mimics the conlleval Perl script) gives precision, recall and F1 of 1.00, while `mode='strict'` with `scheme=IOB2` gives 0.00. Same predictions, two different papers' worth of difference. Always say which mode you used.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Doctrine in public: persistent engagement and responsible cyber power
md: Published doctrine tells you what a state wants to be seen to do, not what it does. The NCF says it does not avow operations, and no state publishes its target list. Treat doctrine as one input to an assessment, alongside observed behaviour, and never as proof of a specific operation.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: North Korea's revenue operations: banks, crypto and IT workers
md: Base checks on verification signals, never on nationality, accent or ethnicity. The schemes used stolen identities of real people, often US citizens, so profiling would both miss them and discriminate against genuine applicants. The question is always "is this person who they say they are, where they say they are?"

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Write NSA and DSA as masked attention and test them against dense
md: This lesson shows no speedup at all: masked attention computes every score, and it ran on a CPU. Speed comes only from kernels that skip unselected blocks, such as the paper's Triton kernel from lesson 4. No GPU timing is shown here; for measured numbers use the paper's A100 results in lesson 4.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
md: The single controller does not mean all tensors flow through one process. Large transfers, especially weight refit, go over channels the controller sets up (CUDA IPC or NCCL), not through the controller itself. A CUDA IPC (inter-process communication) handle is a small token that lets another process on the same machine open the same GPU memory without copying it.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Kaminsky 2008: poisoning a whole domain
md: Kaminsky's insight was economic: random names make every attempt immediately repeatable, and forged delegations make one success worth a whole domain. The fix multiplied the guessing space by about 64,000; only signed data (DNSSEC, next lesson) removes the guessing game entirely.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Intrusion detection, network monitoring, and where to practise
md: Detection is a pipeline: sensors (Suricata, Zeek, flow exporters) produce signals, analysts and rules turn signals into decisions, and the decision must reach someone who acts. Target had the alert; the pipeline broke at the last step.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: JA4 and JARM: fingerprints that survive shuffling, and server scans
md: JARM sends traffic to the server you fingerprint. Scan only servers you own or are authorised to test, or use data from internet scanning services that already publish JARM values. Passive fingerprints (JA3, JA4, JA4S) need nothing but your own sensor.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Layers: the OSI and TCP/IP models, and why both exist
md: Models are maps, not territory. Real protocols do not always fit one layer: ARP (lesson 5) sits between layers 2 and 3, and TLS (Transport Layer Security, the encryption under HTTPS; lesson 12) between 4 and 7. Use the numbers to communicate, not to argue about where a protocol "really" belongs.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Proxies, VPNs and firewalls
md: A VPN is not anonymity and a firewall is not a security boundary for everything. The VPN provider sees what your ISP used to see, and a firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Each control answers one question; know which one.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
md: Simplified model: it ignores caches, assumes perfect overlap, symmetric links and that threads can saturate their controller. Real numbers differ by machine, so measure with your workload. The *ordering* of the options is what the model teaches.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Where candidate boxes come from: proposals, anchors and grids
md: Anchors and grid cells are not predictions. They are fixed reference positions that predictions are expressed relative to. A detector with 20000 anchors does not find 20000 objects; almost all of them are scored as background.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: S3 is not just a slow disk. A disk charges nothing per write and lets you overwrite 4 KiB in place. S3 charges per request, writes whole immutable objects, and takes tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds per request. Every design in this course reshapes writes into **few, large, immutable objects**.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Counts aggregate; quantiles do not. If you want to compute a percentile across instances, regions or time windows later, you must store counts per bucket now. That single decision is why histograms beat summaries almost everywhere.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold
md: Dense text detectors predict a per-pixel map. EAST regresses a box from every text pixel and merges them; DBNet segments shrunk text kernels with a learned threshold, then expands them back.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The reference monitor: one checker that sees every access
md: "We check permissions in the web UI" is not complete mediation. If the API behind the UI, a batch job or a debug endpoint reaches the same data without the check, the monitor is bypassed. Ask of every design: is there any path to the object that skips the checker?

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Virtual machines, containers, gVisor and Firecracker
md: Containers share the host kernel; their strength is the strength of that kernel plus the filters in front of it. VMs give each workload its own kernel and put a small VMM on the boundary. gVisor puts a memory-safe kernel of its own in between. Choose by how untrusted the code is: your own services, other teams' code, or strangers' code.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Search operators: asking a search engine precise questions
md: Run operator searches against your own organisation or a client who has authorised it. Downloading files a search reveals, such as a password list, can itself be unauthorised access or handling of stolen data. Record that the result exists and report it.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Chronolocation: telling the time from shadows
md: Shadow length gives the sun's elevation, shadow direction gives its azimuth, and an astronomical calculation turns both into a time window for a known place and date.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
md: Rebuild cost is decided by the include graph. Touching a header recompiles every translation unit that reaches it, directly or transitively. That is why big projects keep widely included headers small and stable.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
md: A red X on one matrix cell with grey cancelled cells next to it does not mean the other platforms passed. With fail-fast they never finished. Look at which job failed first; that is the one with the real log.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
md: Never reply in anger. Google's guide calls it a serious breach of etiquette that lives forever in the review tool. If a comment stings, ask what constructive point the reviewer is making, and answer that point once you are calm.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Issue first: when to ask, how to report, how to claim work
md: Closing keywords (`close`, `closes`, `closed`, `fix`, `fixes`, `fixed`, `resolve`, `resolves`, `resolved`) only work when the PR targets the repository's **default branch**. Aimed at a release or feature branch, the keyword is ignored and the issue stays open after merge.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebasing replays your commits on a new base. Every replayed commit gets a new hash because its parent changed, even if its diff is identical.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: A license is permission plus conditions. The conditions only apply when you do the thing they attach to, which for most licenses means distributing the code.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
md: A performance claim is an experiment. The PR must let a reviewer rerun it (exact commands, setup, commits) and weigh it (spread, significance and costs), not just read a headline number.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Search that narrows: git grep, ripgrep and word matches
md: GitHub's "find references" is name-based: the docs say it searches all definitions and references across a repository "to find entities with a given name". Two unrelated functions with the same name in different modules will both show up. Check the file and its imports before you trust a reference.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Delta debugging: let a script shrink the repro
md: Automated reduction needs only a yes or no oracle, a check that gives the verdict: does this candidate still show the exact failure? Write that test carefully and the tool does the tedious part.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: Each PR (and each commit in a series) should be justifiable on its own and leave the project building and passing tests. If one depends on another, say so in the description.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Inside the PagedAttention kernel
md: Paging does not make attention read fewer bytes. Every token's key and value are still loaded once per decode step per head; the layout only decides whether those loads are long contiguous runs or scattered pieces, and how many table lookups and masks wrap around them.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Prefix caching never changes outputs. It reuses KV for exactly the same tokens instead of recomputing it, so its effects are on speed and memory (outputs can differ only by the tiny floating-point noise any change in batching causes). It helps exactly as much as prefill dominates the work and prefixes repeat.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Active scanning: host discovery and what each probe tells you
md: Open means a program answered. Closed means the host answered but nothing listens. Filtered means something in between dropped or refused the probe. Open|filtered means silence that could be either. Every state is information about both the host and the firewall in front of it.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: A wide box does not mean each call is slow. It may be cheap but called very often. The flame graph cannot tell the difference because sampling never sees call counts.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Transactions: how libpmemobj's undo log survives a crash
md: A libpmemobj transaction is about crash atomicity, not isolation. The manual is explicit: "transactions do not provide atomicity with respect to other threads". Changes are visible to other threads immediately, so you still need locks (libpmemobj offers persistent-memory-resident mutexes for this).

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Reading headers to triage a suspicious message
md: RFC 8601 says a border server MUST delete any Authentication-Results header that claims its own authserv-id but did not come from a trusted server, and that mail apps should ignore these headers unless the hostname is on an explicit trusted list. Trust exactly one: the topmost from your own authserv-id.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Strict aliasing: which pointer casts C lets you read through
md: "It works in my debug build" proves nothing here. Aliasing bugs are invisible at -O0 and appear only when the optimizer uses the rule, often after an unrelated change lets it inline a function. Like the misaligned cast in lesson 4, the bug is in the source, whatever the build happens to do.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Backbones, top-down versus bottom-up, and part affinity fields
md: Bottom-up is not free of crowd effects. The CNN pass is constant, but the number of candidate pairs per limb grows with the number of people, and the whole image goes through the network at one input size, so small, distant people cover only a few heatmap pixels, while top-down resizes every person to the same crop size.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Inside ML-KEM: modules, compression and the FO transform
md: Name the keys the way FIPS 203 does: **encapsulation key** (ek, public) and **decapsulation key** (dk, secret). ML-KEM.KeyGen starts from two random 32-byte seeds $(d, z)$, and Go's crypto/mlkem stores just this 64-byte seed as the private key; OpenSSL's default private-key file holds the seed plus the expanded decapsulation key. The seed regenerates everything, so protect it exactly like the full decapsulation key.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Filtering during traversal is the right default for medium selectivity, but it has two failure modes at low $s$: a strict walk gets cut off (disconnection), and a walk-through degenerates into visiting about $k/s$ nodes. Both point to the same escape hatch: when matches are few, scan them directly.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: What privacy engineering protects, beyond keeping secrets
md: Privacy engineering reviews every data action, not only every attacker. NIST's objectives give the questions: will people be surprised (predictability), can we find and change or delete one person's data (manageability), and does the system know who is who more than it needs to (disassociability)?

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: When k-anonymity fails: l-diversity and t-closeness
md: l-diversity and t-closeness reduce attribute disclosure in one table under one attacker model. They do not compose across releases and they give no guarantee against unanticipated background knowledge.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Case: the 2020 US Census adopts differential privacy
md: A published epsilon is a starting point for review, not a verdict. Ask what the unit of privacy is, how the budget is split across tables and geographies, and what error users can tolerate. The Census case shows that both privacy and accuracy are political as well as technical choices.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Data protection impact assessments that change the design
md: A DPIA written after launch, or one whose risk section lists only security threats to the company, misses the point. It must be done before processing, assess necessity, and score harm to the individuals in the data.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Windows escalation 1: unquoted paths and weak service permissions
md: Run the path audit and the ACL audit together. An unquoted path with no writable folder before it is a hygiene fix; with one, it is a working escalation to SYSTEM.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Build it: train a small PRM and rerank with it
md: A PRM is a token classifier whose labels sit only on step separators; the rest of the sequence is ignored by the loss. Train and score with identical tokenization, then judge it two ways: does it pick better answers, and does it find the first wrong step.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Linux: every thread is a task, and clone() picks what to share
md: Misconception: "threads are cheap because the kernel treats them as lighter objects." On Linux a thread and a process are the same kind of task. A thread is cheaper to create because there is less to set up (no new address space or page tables), and switching between two threads of one process is cheaper because the address space stays loaded. Those savings come from sharing, not from a different kind of object.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes
md: PQ builds an exponentially large codebook, $(k^*)^m$ centroids, out of $m$ tiny ones. Each vector costs $m \log_2 k^*$ bits no matter how many dimensions it has.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Managed prompt optimizers and a practical workflow
md: A rewrite produced without evaluation data is a hypothesis, not a result. Treat it like a candidate from a proposer: score it on your validation set against the current prompt before shipping.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Text versus bytes: what a computer actually stores
md: Text is characters, bytes are numbers. Decode at the edge of your program (when you read), work with `str` inside, and encode again only when you hash, send or write bytes.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
md: Encoding is reversible formatting, not secrecy. Normalize data (decode, lowercase, refang) before matching it, and expect attackers to stack encodings to slip past exact-match rules.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Expanding with models: doc2query, query2doc and HyDE
md: These numbers come from specific benchmarks (MS MARCO, TREC DL) and specific models. Measure on your own queries with judged results before adopting any expansion: a gain on average can still hurt many individual queries.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: RaBitQ indexing: center and normalize, apply one random rotation, store the sign bits plus two floats per vector. The codebook is the rotated hypercube, so no k-means training is needed.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Workflows as state machines: skipping, repeating and reordering steps
md: Enforce workflows as explicit state machines on the server. For every request ask: is this action allowed from the state this object is in right now? If the only thing enforcing the order is the user interface, the order is not enforced.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Idempotency keys: safe retries, and what they do not stop
md: Look at line four of the output. Idempotency keys are chosen by the client, so an attacker racing a coupon or a withdrawal simply sends a different key with each request. Keys make honest retries safe; they do nothing for limits. The limit itself still needs lesson 9's atomic check.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Paxos: choosing one value with prepare and accept
md: A Paxos proposer is not free to pick its value. After phase 1 it must adopt the value of the highest-numbered proposal any acceptor in its majority reports. That single rule is what keeps a chosen value from ever changing.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Prompting the generator to answer with citations
md: A citation is a claim, not a proof. The model can attach [3] to a sentence [3] does not support, as it did here. ALCE found even the best models lacked complete citation support about 50% of the time on ELI5 (Explain Like I'm Five: open-ended how and why questions from a Reddit forum), so check citations automatically rather than trusting their presence.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: Every cutoff metric hides a choice: the cutoff, the relevance threshold (grade at least 1 here), the divisor, and what to do with short runs. Two papers both reporting "MAP@10" may be computing different numbers.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: The way in: brokers, stolen logins and edge devices
md: MFA is necessary and not sufficient. Session theft (Citrix Bleed), help desk resets and unpatched appliances all walk past a password-plus-code login. Close each door with the control that fits it, and verify by testing, not by policy.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Why sockets cost microseconds and cores, and what RDMA removes
md: RDMA is not "the OS is gone". The kernel driver still creates queues, pins and maps memory, and handles errors. What disappears is per-message kernel work. That split between a slow **control path** and a fast **data path** is the design of the whole API.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: The authoritative server and its fixed tick
md: An authoritative server makes the server state the only truth. Every latency trick in the next lessons changes only what the *client displays*; none of them lets a client decide the outcome.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
md: Do not drop the zeros. Training only on observed implicit events (all with p = 1) lets the model predict 1 everywhere and still reach zero loss. The low-confidence zeros are what make the scores discriminative.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo
md: A common misconception is that the pixels-per-mm method only fails at extreme angles. In this toy, a moderate 40 degree tilt already puts it 15 percent off. Under perspective, scale varies with both position and direction across the plane.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The planner is only as good as its row estimates. It searches join orders exhaustively by dynamic programming up to a limit, then genetically; but a 100x row misestimate can turn the cheapest-looking plan into the slowest. Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE estimates against actuals first.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: A precise test: when is a proxy unhackable?
md: Unhackability is a very strong condition. For rich policy classes, every proxy that is not simply equivalent to the true reward (same ranking of all policies) can be hacked by some policy. Skalse et al. conclude that learned rewards are better treated as aids to policy learning than as specifications to optimize without limit. The practical question becomes how far you can optimize before hacking appears.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: From gaming to tampering: reward tampering and in-context hacking
md: Misconception: reward hacking only happens during RL training. ICRH needs no gradient at all. An agent with frozen weights, a goal and a feedback loop optimizes in context, and its side effects grow with each cycle.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
md: Simulate, do not multiply point estimates. The mean of the simulation is the ALE; the percentiles describe bad years; and a typical year (the median) may cost nothing at all, which is exactly why risk without numbers is easy to ignore until it happens.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: SOC 2: trust services criteria, Type I vs II, and your evidence
md: Read the **exceptions** and the **complementary user entity controls** (CUECs) sections of any vendor's SOC 2. Exceptions are where the auditor found a control did not operate. CUECs are controls the vendor assumes *you* perform (for example, "customers are responsible for enabling MFA for their users"); if you do not, the vendor's report does not cover that risk.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Third-party risk: questionnaires, SBOMs and concentration risk
md: A questionnaire is a vendor's own claims. "Yes" to every question from a 20-person startup is a signal to ask for evidence, not a pass. And a vendor that is excellent at security can still be a concentration risk: CrowdStrike was the security control, not the attacker. Score both "how likely is this vendor to be breached" and "what happens to us if this vendor stops working for a day".

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: A common misconception is that a bigger training cluster speeds up RL roughly linearly. Training is often a minority of the step. If generation is two-thirds of the time, even infinitely fast training saves at most a third.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Training-inference mismatch: same weights, different logprobs
md: "Same checkpoint" does not mean on-policy. Two engines with identical weights are two different policies at the level of logprobs, and the gap grows with FP8 rollout, MoE routing and long sequences. Treat the rollout engine as a behavior policy and log the gap every step.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm
md: Dedup and grouping are lossless: they change how many notifications you receive, not what was observed. Inhibition and silences are lossy: they delete evidence from your view. Use the first two freely and the last two sparingly.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: Do not confuse RRF's k with the k of k-nearest-neighbors. Azure AI Search's docs stress that the RRF constant is "entirely separate" from the k that sets how many neighbors a vector query returns. Elasticsearch names them `rank_constant` and `rank_window_size` to avoid the clash.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: From -ENOMEM and ERR_PTR to Result
md: `to_result` is not a general converter. For a C function that returns a byte count or an index on success, use the raw value: check `< 0` yourself or write a small wrapper that returns `Result<usize>`. Otherwise the success value silently disappears.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The baseline you replace: EEVDF picks and the knobs it offers
md: Misconception: a shorter slice buys a task more CPU. Under EEVDF it buys an earlier deadline and more, shorter turns; the total still follows the weights.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Build, load and run your own scheduler end to end
md: Misconception: the loader is just a launcher and can exit once the scheduler is attached. The link belongs to the process: when it exits, the link is destroyed and the kernel unregisters the scheduler. The loader is also the only place the exit reason gets printed.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
md: Misconception: a lower average latency means a better scheduler. A policy can cut the median and still multiply the p99, and for interactive work the tail is what users feel.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and a signing key that should have died in 2021
md: A signing key's real lifetime is not what the plan says but what the system enforces. Enforce expiry in code, alert on key age, and treat "we paused rotation" as a security incident with an owner and a deadline.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
md: Pollution is process-wide and lasts until restart. One request can change the behaviour of every later request to that Node.js process, including other users' requests, which makes it confusing to debug and dangerous to leave running.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Heartbleed as a diff: reviewing every field of a message
md: Field checklist for any parser diff: list every value taken from outside, and for each one point to the line that validates it against a fact the code controls (the real buffer length, a maximum). An empty cell is a finding. For pointer loops, end checks use < or >=, never == or !=.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Secure channels at every layer: what each protocol protects
md: Ask two questions of any secure protocol: between which two points does the protection start and stop, and what happens to the data outside them? A VPN stops at the gateway; SSH stops at the server process; S/MIME never stops while the message stays encrypted.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Time is a security input: NTP, delay attacks and NTS
md: NTS stops forged and altered time replies; it cannot stop delay attacks, because a delayed packet is still authentic. RFC 8915 bounds the damage at MAXDIST/2 and suggests several time sources or several network paths. Combine NTS with multiple servers and alert on large clock steps.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The perimeter model, Operation Aurora and the road to BeyondCorp
md: Zero trust does not mean "no VPN" or "no firewall". BeyondCorp removed the trust that came with being on the network. Encrypted tunnels and network filters still exist in zero trust designs; they just stop being the reason anyone gets access.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Measuring the journey: CISA's maturity model and a migration plan
md: A maturity score measures capabilities, not outcomes. An agency can be Advanced in every pillar and still be breached through an unpatched edge appliance. Track both: the stage per pillar, and evidence such as how many apps still need a VPN and how many accounts still use phishable MFA.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Worked scenario: prompt injection through attacker-written log fields
md: Anything an attacker can write into a log can end up in your model's context. Give the model no authority the attacker should not have, let deterministic rules make decisions, and treat instruction-like text in a field as an indicator.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors
md: Attack surface is everything an attacker can touch: services, features, trust relationships and people. The Morris worm used all four kinds at once. The cheapest defence is removing doors you do not need (a debug command in production, an unused service); the next is making each remaining door check its input.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
md: Real attacks do not walk the phases neatly in order. Attackers loop (discover, move, discover again), skip steps (a stolen password needs no weaponization), and run phases in parallel. Use the models as a vocabulary and a checklist, not a script.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Building a programme from zero: the first 90 days
md: Do not promise a compliance date (a SOC 2 report, an ISO certificate) before you know the current state. Recall that SOC 2 Type II needs a period of operating evidence: a date picked in week one becomes a commitment you may have to break publicly.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Metrics that drive decisions, and how targets corrupt them
md: Choose a few metrics that map to decisions: implementation for rollout, effectiveness and efficiency for whether controls work, impact for executives. Pair each target with a metric that would reveal gaming, measure what is still open, and make the things that matter part of how leaders are judged.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Rebuilding after failure: Equifax, Maersk and Microsoft
md: Beware survivorship and self-reporting. You read about rebuilds that companies chose to describe; failed rebuilds rarely get Senate testimony. Figures such as "35,000 engineers" or "USD 1.25 billion" are the companies' own, with their own definitions. Use them as examples of levers, not as benchmarks.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Getting a fix shipped when you cannot order it
md: Escalation is not a weapon. If owners learn that talking to security means being reported upward, they stop talking to security, and you lose the early warnings that matter most. Agree the path in advance, use it predictably, and make the first step always a direct conversation.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Build a STaR loop: sample, filter, fine-tune, repeat
md: Measure the filter, not just the score. Two cheap audits caught what accuracy alone hid: check an intermediate quantity on a sample of kept data, and track held-out accuracy every iteration, since training accuracy rises regardless.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Choosing the threshold: hit rate against false hits
md: Do not copy a threshold from a tutorial or a library default. Collect a few hundred real pairs from your traffic, label whether the cached answer would be correct, and pick the threshold from that data and your cost of a wrong answer. Re-check whenever you change the embedding model, since similarity scales differ between models.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Validating outbound URLs in code
md: Validate the *destination*, not the *string*: fixed scheme, allowlisted host, resolved IP checked against private ranges, the connection pinned to that IP, and no automatic redirects. Then assume the check will one day fail and limit what the network lets the server reach.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: HiCache: a radix tree that spans GPU, host memory and storage
md: Misconception: "a large `--hicache-ratio` pools the host memory of all my servers." It only makes each instance's own L2 bigger. Cross-instance reuse needs a shared L3 backend, and the router must still send related requests where the KV is cheapest to reach.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
md: A road network is a large, sparse, directed graph with **nonnegative** weights. Every fast routing algorithm in this course depends on the weights never being negative.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The DFT: one dot product per complex sinusoid
md: The DFT is a matrix-vector product: $N$ dot products of the signal with orthogonal complex sinusoids. Each $X[k]$ says how much of frequency $k$ is present (magnitude) and where it starts (phase), and the inverse DFT rebuilds $x$ exactly.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
md: Misconception: "my SIMD loop is slow, so I need wider vectors." If it streams from DRAM with little math per byte, it is memory-bound and AVX-512 will not help. Measure bytes per second against your machine's bandwidth first.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The buddy allocator: split in halves, merge with one XOR
md: Buddy trades internal fragmentation (power-of-two rounding, up to about 50 percent) for fast, simple coalescing: the buddy is one XOR away. It suits page-granular, physically contiguous memory, which is why Linux uses it for its page allocator and builds smaller allocators on top.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Low-precision rollout: FP8 weights, FP8 KV cache and INT4
md: Low precision in slime is a rollout-side copy: train in bf16, serve FP8 from a converted checkpoint whose `quantization_config` the trainer reuses at every sync. The price is that SGLang now samples from a rounded policy, a gap between rollout and trainer probabilities that lesson 8 measures and corrects.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Is the run working? Evaluation, metrics, checkpoints and recovery
md: Recovery has limits. Without straw or rollout dumps you keep the engines but cannot replay batches after the last checkpoint. If the ServingCluster actor or the whole Ray cluster is lost, you start serving again and resume from the checkpoint; node loss and preemption need your scheduler's help. A resume with a different TP or PP layout reinitializes RNG, so it is not bitwise identical.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: A toy chain in Python, and thinking in invariants
md: Before reading any contract, write down its invariants: "holds at least what it owes", "total shares match total assets", "only the owner can change the owner". Every bug class that follows is a way to break one of them.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The alert lifecycle, and why the queue is not first come, first served
md: Allow-listing the scanner fixes the noise but creates a blind spot: an attacker on that address is now invisible to the rule. The NCSC says allow lists must be "strongly object/time bounded" (one address, its scheduled window, an expiry date) "to minimise the risk of perpetual allow listing and the evasion of monitoring".

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Cloud key misuse, and what Snowflake customers could see in 2024
md: Cloud and SaaS triage starts with three questions: what kind of credential is this, where is it being used from compared with normal, and what did it touch. The third question can only be answered if the right logs (S3 data events, the warehouse's query history) were switched on and kept long enough before the incident.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Password and MFA friction: rules that backfire and rules that work
md: Misconception: "more password rules means more security". Composition rules and forced changes make people choose predictable variants and write them down. Length, a blocklist, rate limiting, and MFA that is bound to the site do the real work.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Testing the people layer: rules of engagement, ethics and metrics
md: Test processes, not people. Authorise every site with whoever controls it, plan for police, review lures for harm, report without names, and measure reporting speed and procedure compliance rather than click counts.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: A latent dying is not the same as a feature being absent from the model. It only means this SAE found no use for that column, often because of optimisation, not because the concept is missing.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Every interpolator here is a weighted average $\sum_i \lambda_i z_i$. The only question is how to pick the weights. Keep this frame: the rest of the course compares weight recipes on the same six sensors.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Kriging is the best linear unbiased predictor (linear: a weighted sum of readings; unbiased: weights sum to 1; best: smallest error variance) only under its own model. With few points, an unreliable variogram can make it worse than IDW, as in this toy. Its variance map is only as trustworthy as the variogram, so check calibration with standardized LOO errors.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts and prompt lookup decoding
md: All variants share one loop: draft cheaply (small model, extra heads, feature-level head, or string lookup), verify a chain or tree in one target pass, keep the accepted prefix plus one target token. They differ only in how they guess, and that sets alpha and c.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
md: Silence is where a language-model decoder is least constrained by audio. Short clips are padded to 30 s, long pauses leave long stretches of nothing, and the decoder can fill them with plausible web-caption text. The repetition and confidence checks do not catch a fluent, confident invented sentence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Beyond the basic chunk: size classes, thread caches and fragmentation
md: Thread caches are a memory-for-speed trade. jemalloc's manual says it plainly: caching makes allocation very fast but increases memory use and fragmentation, since some objects stay parked in each thread's cache. TCMalloc moved to per-CPU caches because per-thread caches made footprint grow with the number of threads.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
md: Little free memory is not a problem by itself. The page cache deliberately fills idle RAM with file data, and clean cached pages are reclaimable at any moment. Trouble shows up as rates: sustained swap-in and swap-out in `vmstat`, major faults per second, and processes stalled in direct reclaim.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
md: Window by **event time** (when the device measured) whenever the result should describe the physical world. Processing time describes your pipeline, not your sensor: a network hiccup would change a temperature average.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: Misconception: "QoS 2 at the device makes the pipeline exactly-once". MQTT QoS covers one hop. The bridge, Kafka producer, stream job and sink each need their own guarantee, and a single at-least-once hop reintroduces duplicates.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
md: "Attention is all you need" does not mean attention is all there is. Without the FFN, residual connections, normalization and positional encodings, a stack of attention layers loses most of its parameters, its sense of order, and its trainability.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
md: Saturation does not mean repeated terms are ignored. With k1 = 1.2, going from 1 to 2 occurrences still raises the factor from 0.45 to 0.62. It means each extra occurrence is worth less than the one before, with a hard ceiling.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
md: Pre-LN vs post-LN is not cosmetic. Xiong et al. show that in the original post-LN Transformer the gradients near the output are large at initialization, which is why it needs a careful learning-rate warmup. Placing LayerNorm inside the residual branch, as GPT-2 does, gives well-behaved gradients at initialization.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
md: $f'(x)$ answers: if I nudge $x$ by a tiny amount, how many times that amount does $f$ change? Positive means $f$ rises to the right, negative means it falls, zero means the tangent is flat.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: The gradient gives the direction; the learning rate decides the distance. The largest stable learning rate is set by the **steepest** direction of the loss, while progress in the **shallowest** direction decides how long training takes.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
md: A command runs in a **copy** of the shell. It inherits open files, the working directory and exported variables, and nothing it changes flows back. Only builtins and functions run inside the shell itself.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk
md: grep selects lines, sed rewrites them, awk computes over fields, and find selects files. Single-quote every pattern so the shell leaves it alone, and add `-E` when you want `+`, `?`, `|` or groups.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
md: An embedding is a learned weight matrix indexed by item ID. Meaning is not built in: the vectors start random and become useful only because some training objective rewards putting related items close together. The rest of this course is about which objectives do that.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Contrastive training in practice: in-batch negatives and collapse
md: A falling contrastive loss is not proof of a good representation: a model can solve the training task with features that transfer poorly, as SimCLR's normalization ablation shows. Track a downstream measure such as linear evaluation, and check for collapse by looking at the spread of the embeddings.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
md: Reserving the maximum length for every request wastes most of the cache. vLLM's profiling found only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV memory held actual token states in earlier systems, due to reserved slots and fragmentation. PagedAttention fixes this by allocating the cache in small fixed-size blocks, like OS pages.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: A **program** is a file of bytes on disk. A **process** is a running instance of it: its own memory (code, data, heap, stack), its own register values (the CPU's working slots, lesson 3), and OS bookkeeping such as open files. One program can be running as many processes at once.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: `call` = push return address + jump. `ret` = pop into the program counter. Everything a function keeps on the stack lives only until it returns, which is why the stack can be reused so cheaply.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
md: Same network, three different training signals: raw text (what comes next?), demonstrations (what would a good assistant write?), and comparisons (which of these two answers is better?). Each stage starts from the weights of the previous one.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Where preference data comes from: guidelines, safety, AI feedback
md: AI feedback moves the specification, it does not remove it. The labels are only as good as the feedback model and the principles, and a model judging a model can share its blind spots. Teams still check AI-labeled preferences and the resulting policy against human judgments.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
md: Intersection is a linear merge over sorted lists. Make it cheap by starting from the rarest term, and make long lists skippable.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
md: A header declaring a function is not the same as the function existing. `#include` only pastes a promise into your file. If the definition lives in `area.c` (or a library), it must also reach the linker, or the build fails at link time with an undefined symbol error even though every file compiled cleanly.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Integer types and conversions: where -1 > 0u
md: Never compare a signed value with an unsigned one without thinking about negatives. `if (len < cap)` with `int len = -1` and `size_t cap = 16` is false on LP64 systems: len converts to a huge size_t. Keep lengths and indexes in size_t throughout, or check for negatives before comparing.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Files and errors: stdio, return codes and errno
md: Do not test errno to find out whether a call failed. A successful call may leave errno nonzero from some earlier, unrelated failure, or even set it itself. Test the return value; consult errno only after the return value reports failure.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership is not about the stack versus the heap as such. A `String` header can live on the stack, in a `Vec` (Rust's growable array), or inside a struct field; wherever it lives, that location is the owner, and the heap block is freed when that owner is dropped.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Structs that borrow: lifetimes in types and what 'static means
md: `T: 'static` does not mean the value lives forever. An owned `String` satisfies the bound and is still dropped at the end of its owner's scope. The bound only says the receiver may keep the value as long as it likes, because nothing inside it can dangle. `thread::spawn` puts this bound on its closure (lesson 10).

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
md: A dot product of 0 does not mean the vectors are unrelated in every sense; it means they are **perpendicular** (orthogonal). And a big dot product does not by itself mean similar direction: it can come from long vectors. When you want direction only, normalize first or use cosine.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Orthogonality, projections and least squares
md: Orthogonal matrices keep lengths and angles, and $Q^{-1} = Q^\top$. Projecting $\mathbf{b}$ onto a line or a column space leaves a residual orthogonal to it, and that orthogonality condition, $X^\top(\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0}$, is least squares.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: The loss you minimize is computed on the **training** data, but what you actually care about is performance on new data. Lessons 6 to 9 show how these two come apart, and what to do about it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
md: Zero training error is not proof of a good model, and not proof of a bad one either. The degree-9 fit has zero training error and poor test error; lesson 9 shows that large modern networks can also hit zero training error and still generalize.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
md: Fit everything (scalers, feature selection, imputation) inside the training fold, ideally with a Pipeline. Split by group or by time when rows are related. Expect distribution shift in deployment, and always report a trivial baseline next to your model.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Multi-class outputs: softmax, logits and the p minus y gradient
md: Misconception: raising one logit only raises its own probability. The Jacobian's off-diagonal entries $-p_i p_j$ are negative, so every other probability falls (they must still sum to 1). That is why a wrong class's logit gets the positive gradient $p_j$ even though the loss $-\ln p_y$ reads only the true class: $p_y$ depends on every logit through the softmax denominator.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: A system call is not just a function call. It looks like one because the C library wraps it, but inside is a trap that changes privilege level, and the kernel, not the caller, decides which code runs.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
md: A condition variable has no memory: signaling when nobody waits does nothing. That is why the waiting thread must check a state variable before it sleeps, rather than relying on catching the signal.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Describing data: mean, median, percentiles and outliers
md: Percentiles do not average. The p99 of two servers combined is not the mean of their two p99 values: it depends on how many requests each served and on the shape of both tails. Compute percentiles from the merged raw data (or from merged histograms).

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Continuous variables: densities, CDFs and common distributions
md: A density value is not a probability. A density of 2 does not mean probability 2, and the probability of any single exact value is 0, which is why $<$ and $\le$ give the same answer for continuous variables.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
md: Prior plus data gives a posterior. MAP is maximum likelihood plus a log-prior term, which is why L2 and L1 penalties are Gaussian and Laplace priors in disguise.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
md: Compute-optimal training scales model size and data **together**, each roughly as the square root of compute. The rule of thumb that falls out is about 20 training tokens per parameter.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
md: P@k does not average well across queries. If a query has only 3 relevant documents, even a perfect system gets P@10 = 0.3. Also note that trec_eval's P@k pads short result lists with nonrelevant documents: retrieving 15 documents with 4 relevant gives P@20 = 4/20 = 0.2.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
md: Pooling a pretrained language model does not give you a good embedding model. BERT was never trained to make cosine meaningful; the training objective in the next lesson is what does that.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: Ties are common on small data. This code picks the pair it encountered first, so a different tie-break or a different word order can produce a different merge list. Real trainers fix a deterministic rule; production implementations also update pair counts incrementally instead of recounting everything, as Sennrich et al. note.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: WordPiece, Unigram and SentencePiece in depth
md: BPE replays merges in learned order. WordPiece scores merges by count(ab) / (count(a) count(b)) and encodes by longest match. Unigram prunes a big vocabulary by likelihood and segments with Viterbi. SentencePiece runs BPE or Unigram on raw text with the space as a symbol.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Batch size, gradient accumulation and tuning hyperparameters
md: Batch size sets the speed; the learning rate decides whether you train at all. Tune the learning rate first, on a log scale: a range test finds the decade, random trials refine it. When you accumulate gradients, divide each micro-batch loss by the number of micro-batches.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
md: Tune HNSW in this order: pick M for your data (12 to 48 is typical), set ef_construction high enough that build-time recall is near 1, then sweep ef at query time against brute-force ground truth until recall@k meets your target at acceptable latency.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Signing artifacts: from long-lived keys to Sigstore
md: Verifying 'signed by somebody' proves nothing: an attacker can get a valid Sigstore certificate for their own identity in seconds. The security comes from `--certificate-identity` and `--certificate-oidc-issuer`, which you must set to the one workflow or person you actually expect.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity
md: Three of these metrics only look inside the generated set: a generator can be varied in phrasing while missing whole topics. Only rare-slice coverage compares against real data, so keep a held-out real set. Also compare sets of equal size and length; distinct-n falls as texts get longer even with no loss of diversity, and 5-sentence sets like these are noisy.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: vdso(7) states that calls served by the vDSO do not appear in `strace` output (strace is a tool that prints every system call a process makes) and are invisible to seccomp filters (seccomp, secure computing mode, lets a process restrict which system calls it may make). A trace with zero `clock_gettime` lines does not mean the program never asks for the time.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Shared memory between processes: MAP_SHARED, shm_open and memfd
md: The ring spins while it waits, burning a whole CPU. Real shared-memory queues sleep when empty or full, for example on a POSIX semaphore placed in the shared region, as shm_overview(7) suggests, and use spinning at most for a short time first.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Coordinated omission: the load tester stops looking when it hurts
md: Coordinated omission does not make individual samples wrong: the 2 ms readings were real. The bug is which samples exist. The tester samples less often precisely when the server is slow, so the sample set is biased toward good moments. No statistic computed afterwards can recover samples that were never taken.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: IMSI catchers and false base stations: downgrade and detection
md: Turning on 5G does not remove the 2G risk by itself. As long as the phone will still accept 2G, an attacker can try to push it there. Disabling 2G on the device is what closes the fallback.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Case: the Viasat KA-SAT attack (24 February 2022)
md: KA-SAT was hit through its ground segment: a VPN appliance, a trusted management network and legitimate commands sent at scale. Protect the management plane like the product itself, and limit how much any single command can break.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
md: Every time-scoped question becomes interval arithmetic once two things are fixed: the reference date, and the convention for partial dates. Allen relations, current-role tests and window clipping are all a few endpoint comparisons.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Verifiers set the ceiling: error rates, GenRM and self-verification
md: Self-verification is not free precision. The same paper finds that frontier models have remarkably weak verification out of the box and needed these prompting strategies (and introduces a benchmark for it). Before scaling N, measure your verifier's true and false positive rates on your own samples.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Measure it yourself: a test-time scaling harness on GSM8K
md: A scaling harness is three numbers per question and $k$: coverage, what your selection rule achieves, and the gap between them, split by difficulty. The gap tells you how much a better verifier could buy; the bins tell you where to spend the budget.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Large-chunk TTT, one map of the design space, and the costs
md: Learned memory turns the state of a recurrent layer into a model trained online. You choose its architecture, objective, forgetting and optimizer; you pay for expressiveness in wall-clock time, and you still pair it with attention for exact local recall.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Three ways to start a hunt: hypothesis, intelligence and data
md: A hypothesis that cannot fail is not a hypothesis. "Something bad may be happening somewhere" will consume a week and conclude nothing. Name the behaviour, the place and the data. A disproved hypothesis is a useful result: it is evidence that one specific attack path is not in use, at least in the data you have.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: What threat intelligence is, and what it is for
md: Threat intelligence is threat information that has been analysed and put in context **for a decision**. If you cannot name the decision a product supports, you are not yet producing intelligence.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Sharing at machine speed: TAXII, MISP and communities
md: Automated sharing amplifies errors as fast as it spreads truth. Before publishing, check values against warning lists, set `to_ids` only on values safe to block, add an expiry or decay model, and never publish an indicator you have not graded.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: STRIDE per element: from a diagram to a threat list
md: STRIDE per element checks parts, not their combination. The 2006 article admits that threats frequently materialise only when systems are joined, because combining them violates assumptions each part made. Always ask what changes when this system is connected to the next one.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers
md: Tiering wins only if the *hot* pages live in the fast tier. The capacity of each tier matters less than the fraction of accesses it serves. Everything in this course is machinery for keeping $h$ high cheaply.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Honest evaluation: error metrics, MASE and rolling origins
md: Report a forecast's accuracy as an average over many origins, at the horizon you will use in production, with a scaled metric such as MASE next to seasonal naive. A single train/test split can rank two methods either way by luck.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Certificate authorities, the CA/Browser Forum and ACME
md: Domain validation proves control of a name at one moment, nothing more. Anyone who can control your DNS or your web server's port 80 for a few minutes can get a valid certificate for your domain. That is why CAA, multi-perspective validation and CT monitoring exist.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
md: Fusion in Triton is mostly a matter of keeping a tile in registers between operations. Load once, do every elementwise op and reduction on the block, store once.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
md: GenEval prompts are short and templated, and some models are trained mostly on long synthetic captions. Emu3's authors say exactly this and report rewriter numbers too. Before comparing two papers, check the rewriter, the CFG scale, and whether numbers were measured or copied from another paper.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Concurrency in one address space: cooperative threads and no fork
